newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Gujarat Ambuja H1 profits seen up 16-22 pct.
newsitem.headline: India's Gujarat Ambuja H1 profits seen up 16-22 pct.

text.p: India's Gujarat Ambuja Cement is expected to show a 16-22 percent rise in net profits for the first half ending December 1996 but a prolonged slump in cement prices could end up stunting growth for the full year, analysts said on Tuesday.
The company, India's fourth largest cement firm, is due to announce its first half 1996/97 results on Wednesday.
Analysts said they expect Gujarat Ambuja to report a net profit between 475-500 million rupees ($13.2-$13.9 million) in first half 1996/97 against a net of 409.7 million in the year-ago period.
"We forecast a net profit of about 515 million rupees with high volume growth spearheading the company's performance," said a cement analyst at an Indian associate of a U.S. securities firm.

Full operational benefits of multilocational cement plants in the northern states of Himachal Pradesh and Punjab, started in October 1995, are expected to drive superior volumes as compared to industry peers, analysts said.

"The firm has shown a 95 percent growth in despatches in the first four months of the current year beginning July. This is mainly due to the new capacity which was not there in most of the first half last year," James Capel B&K said in its latest January update on the company.
"We forecast a net profit of 480-500 million rupees. Volume growth will help the firm," said Ruchira Katyal, cement analyst at securities firm Hoare Govett (India) Securities Ltd.
Katyal said the profit estimate excluded provision for a new minimum tax enforced by the government in its July 1996 budget.
Moves by the government to exempt firms with units in backward areas from a new Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) imposed on "zero-tax paying companies will help the company, analysts said.
"The firm's effective tax rate will be about 10 percent instead of 12.9 percent MAT," said cement analyst Ravi Sundararaman at JM Share & Stock Brokers.
Company sales for the six months ending December are forecast at 3.5 billion to 3.8 billion rupees, up by 30-40 percent over the corresponding period, analysts said.

Analysts said a slowdown in the construction sector that has led to an oversupply in some key cement markets would hurt the performances of cement companies like Gujarat Ambuja over the full 1996/97 year, however.

Cement prices have remained flat around 140-150 rupees per 50 kg bag in Bombay during the period despite a substantial rise in the cost of production caused by increased power and freight costs, analysts said. Prices have also fallen in Gujarat, another of Ambuja's leading markets.
"Gujarat Ambuja has been consistently underperforming against the Bombay's benchmark 30-share index and sentiment to the industry is still bearish," Govett's Katyal said.
But, some firms are still upbeat on cement stocks.
Global investment bank Lehman Brothers last week advised investors to selectively shift towards cyclicals such as cement and construction from stable sectors.
The firm said it had increased its weighting of Gujarat Ambuja Cement, adding that cement shares had underperformed the market for the past year by more than 30 percentage points.
Analysts say Ambuja would continue to show strong operating profit margins of about 35-37 percent, reflecting good quality earnings.
"The major advantage of Ambuja is its high operating margins," James Capel said.
Analysts describe Gujarat Ambuja as India's most efficient cement producer.
